content: The document outlines the terms and conditions for the use, adaptation, and redistribution of a World Health Organization (WHO) publication. WHO is not liable for damages arising from its use. The document is part of WHO’s guidelines on viral hepatitis planning and tracking progress toward elimination. It was developed for transparency and information purposes, as required by WHO’s guideline development process. The document acknowledges contributions from Dr. Yvan Hutin of the Global Hepatitis Programme and members of the scientific committee from WHO’s six regions, who provided comments and suggestions. It also credits Marc Rondy for coordinating the peer-review process and submitting the protocol to the ethics committee. The document includes a list of acronyms and abbreviations used throughout, such as CI (confidence interval), CLIA (chemiluminescence assay), DBS (dried blood spot), and others related to hepatitis biomarkers and diagnostic methods. The protocol provides a framework for conducting biomarker surveys to estimate the prevalence of infection with hepatitis viruses (HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV, HEV). It outlines key questions to adapt the protocol to national needs, such as which hepatitis viruses require prevalence estimates, the target populations, and the characteristics of interest (e.g., age, gender). It also addresses sampling methods, specimen collection techniques, diagnostic methods, and strategies for returning results to participants. The primary objectives of the biomarker survey include estimating the prevalence of serological evidence of past or present infection with HAV, HEV, HBV, HDV, and HCV, as well as chronic infections. Secondary objectives include estimating the proportion of individuals with chronic HBV or HCV infection who are aware of their status and assessing the prevalence of specific biomarkers (e.g., HBeAg, HBV DNA). The survey design is cross-sectional, and the study population may include the general population or specific groups with higher prevalence rates (e.g., people who inject drugs, healthcare workers, sex workers). Sampling strategies include simple random sampling, systematic sampling, and cluster sampling, with an emphasis on avoiding non-representative methods like convenience sampling. Specimen collection techniques include venepuncture, capillary blood sampling, and dried blood spots. Diagnostic methods may involve rapid diagnostic tests or laboratory-based in vitro diagnostics. The survey will also consider synergies with other health programs, such as HIV or immunization initiatives. Operational definitions for case identification are based on WHO-recommended criteria, such as the presence of specific antibodies or antigens for each hepatitis virus. The document provides detailed guidance on sampling procedures, including the use of random number generators, systematic selection of individuals, and cluster sampling within communities. Fieldworkers will enumerate individuals in selected households and collect data accordingly. The protocol emphasizes the importance of collecting sufficient blood specimens and ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the data. It is designed to guide national stakeholders in conducting biomarker surveys to inform hepatitis elimination strategies and assess the impact of vaccination and other interventions.
